title: The Past Simple
summary: The *būtasis kartinis laikas*: one past tense doing the work of the English simple past, perfect and continuous together. It has two sets of endings, and which of them a verb takes is settled by the third form given in the dictionary.

rules.heading: The Third Principal Part
rules.statement: Every Lithuanian verb is cited with **three** forms — *dirbti, dirba, dirbo* — and the third of them is the past. It is not derivable from the other two, which is exactly why the dictionary gives it: the past stem must be learnt with the verb, as the present stem was (¶35). Once it is known, the whole tense follows, because the past has only **two** patterns of ending against the present's three.

paradigms.caption: The three principal parts
paradigms.footnote: The present type and the past type are independent: *valgyti* is a third-conjugation present and an *-ė* past, *kalbėti* a second-conjugation present and an *-o* past. Knowing one tells you nothing about the other.

rules.heading: The Past of the -o Type
rules.statement: Where the third principal part ends in **-o**, the personal endings are those below. Cut the *-o* from the cited form and add them; the third person is the cited form itself, and serves both numbers as it does in the present (¶57).

paradigms.caption: dirbti, dirba, dirbo — past
paradigms.footnote: So too *ėjau, ėjai, ėjo, ėjome, ėjote, ėjo* and *kalbėjau, kalbėjai, kalbėjo, kalbėjome, kalbėjote, kalbėjo*.

examples.gloss: Last year we lived in Kaunas.
Did you speak to the teacher?

rules.heading: The Past of the -ė Type
rules.statement: Where the third principal part ends in **-ė**, the endings differ in the first and second person singular: **-iau** and **-ei**. The *-iau* is a back vowel, and it therefore softens a preceding **t** to *č* and **d** to *dž*, exactly as the genitive does (¶28) — *skaitė* gives *skaičiau*, not *skaitiau*.

paradigms.caption: skaityti, skaito, skaitė — past
paradigms.footnote: Likewise *matė → mačiau*, *valgė → valgiau*, *rašė → rašiau*. The softening happens only before *-iau*; the other five forms keep the consonant unaltered.

rules.heading: The Past of Būti
rules.statement: **Būti** is regular in the past, whatever it does in the present: its third principal part is *buvo*, and the *-o* endings of ¶89 apply without exception. Note that where the present tense may drop *yra* altogether (¶16), the past may **not** — *buvo* has to be said.

examples.note: the predicate noun stands in the nominative, as in the present (¶16)

rules.heading: Negation in the Past
rules.statement: Negation works in the past exactly as in the present: **ne-** is written onto the front of the verb as one word (¶25), and the object of the negated verb goes into the **genitive** (¶26). Nothing about the past tense alters either rule — which is worth stating plainly, because learners commonly keep the accusative once the sentence moves out of the present.

examples.gloss: She did not read the book.

rules.heading: Telling What Happened
rules.statement: The one past tense covers what English divides among three: *dirbau* is *I worked*, *I was working* and *I have worked* alike, and the context or an adverb supplies the difference. The adverbs that most often supply it are **vakar** (yesterday), **pernai** (last year) and **prieš** with the accusative (¶87). This is also the tense of a biography — where one was born, where one studied, where one worked.

rows.label: continuous
cells: When you rang, I was working.

rows.label: perfect
cells: I have already worked in Lithuania.

examples.target: Studijavau universitete, o paskui dirbau mokykloje.
examples.gloss: I studied at the university, and afterwards worked at a school.
A year ago I came to Lithuania.

drills.explanation: The third principal part *dirbo* is an *-o* past, so the first person singular is **dirbau**. *dirbu* is the present, *dirbo* the third person, *dirbome* the first person plural.

drills.stem: Complete: **Vakar ____ namie.** (Yesterday I was at home.)
drills.explanation: *būti* has *buvo* for its third principal part and takes the *-o* endings: *buvau*. Unlike the present, where *yra* may be dropped, the past tense of *būti* must be said.
An *-ė* past takes **-iau** in the first person singular, and the *-iau* softens the preceding **t** to *č*: *skaičiau*. *skaitau* is the present.
*mačiau* (from *matė*) and *valgėme* (from *valgė*) are past; *matau* and *gyvena* are present. The softening in *mačiau* is the mark of the *-iau* ending.

drills.stem: Complete: **Ji neskaitė ____.** (She did not read the book.)
drills.explanation: The object of a negated verb stands in the genitive, and the past tense changes nothing about that: *knygos*. Keeping the accusative *knygą* after a negative is one of the commonest errors of the level.

drills.stem: Why can *dirbau* be translated three different ways in English?
options: Because it is ambiguous between persons.
Because Lithuanian has one past tense where English distinguishes simple, continuous and perfect.
Because it may also be a present.
Because the ending -au belongs to two conjugations.
drills.explanation: *I worked*, *I was working* and *I have worked* are all *dirbau*; an adverb or the context supplies whatever difference is wanted. The same economy was seen in the present (¶24).

drills.stem: Which statements about the past tense are correct?
options: The third person serves both singular and plural.
There are two sets of endings, -o and -ė.
The past type can be predicted from the conjugation of the present.
Negation is written onto the verb as one word.
drills.explanation: Present type and past type are independent — *valgyti* has a third-conjugation present and an *-ė* past, *kalbėti* a second-conjugation present and an *-o* past. That is why the dictionary gives all three forms.

drills.stem: **rašyti, rašo, rašė.** Which form is the second person singular past?
drills.explanation: An *-ė* past takes **-ei** in the second person singular: *rašei*. *rašai* is the present, *rašiau* the first person past, *rašėte* the second person plural.

drills.stem: **Jis buvo mokytojas.** Why is *mokytojas* not in the accusative?
options: Because a predicate noun after *būti* stands in the nominative, in the past as in the present.
Because the past tense governs the nominative.
drills.explanation: *Būti* links rather than governs, so what follows it names the subject again and stands in the nominative (¶16). The tense makes no difference to this.

drills.stem: How many **distinct** written forms does a Lithuanian verb have in the past tense across all six persons?
drills.explanation: Five: the third person is one form serving both numbers, so *dirbau, dirbai, dirbo, dirbome, dirbote* exhaust the paradigm. The same economy holds in the present (¶57), and it is why Lithuanian tolerates dropping the pronoun so freely.

drills.title: Trumpa biografija
drills.passage: Gimiau tūkstantis devyni šimtai devyniasdešimt penktaisiais metais Kaune. Ten gyvenau dešimt metų. Paskui mes atvažiavome į Vilnių, ir aš studijavau universitete. Vakarais dirbau kavinėje ir skaičiau knygas. Pernai nedirbau — buvau namie ir mokiausi lietuvių kalbos. Vakar mačiau seną draugą; mes kalbėjome apie mokyklą.
drills.translation: I was born in 1995 in Kaunas. I lived there for ten years. Then we came to Vilnius, and I studied at the university. In the evenings I worked in a café and read books. Last year I did not work — I was at home and studied Lithuanian. Yesterday I saw an old friend; we talked about school.

questions.explanation: *Gimiau … Kaune.* The move to Vilnius came ten years later. *Kaune* is a locative of place (¶59).

questions.stem: Which verbs in the passage belong to the **-ė** past type?
questions.explanation: *matė* and *skaitė* are *-ė* pasts, and both show the softening before *-iau*. *dirbo* and *kalbėjo* are *-o* pasts, which is why they give *dirbau* and *kalbėjome* with no consonant change.

questions.stem: For how many years did the writer live in Kaunas?
questions.explanation: *Ten gyvenau dešimt metų* — ten. *dešimt* fixes *metai* in the genitive plural (¶80), and the phrase as a whole is a stretch of time, which Lithuanian expresses without any word answering to English *for*.
